author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduction to Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory using Methane.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number.
instructions: Listen to the narration and observe the 3D structure of methane.

clips.changeMeaning: Show methane molecule and introduce basic VSEPR concept
clips.narration: Welcome to the VSEPR Theory lab. VSEPR stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion. The core idea is that electron domains around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize mutual repulsion. Let's start with methane, CH4.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight tetrahedral geometry and 109.5 degree bond angles
clips.narration: Methane has four bonding pairs of electrons around the central carbon atom. To get as far apart from each other as possible in 3D space, they form a tetrahedral geometry. Notice the bond angles are exactly 109.5 degrees.

modules.description: Exploring how lone pairs alter molecular geometry and bond angles using Ammonia and Water.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
instructions: Observe how the presence of lone pairs changes the physical shape of the molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Show ammonia molecule to introduce lone pair effects
clips.narration: Now consider Ammonia, NH3. It also has a steric number of four, but one domain is a non-bonding lone pair. Because lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, they push the hydrogen atoms closer together.
Next is water, H2O. The oxygen atom has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry is 'bent'.

clips.changeMeaning: Compare bond angles of NH3 and H2O, adding rotation to observe 3D shapes
clips.narration: The additional lone pair in water causes even greater repulsion. While methane's angles are 109.5 degrees, ammonia is compressed to 107 degrees, and water's bond angle is squeezed down to 104.5 degrees.

modules.description: Investigating 5 and 6 electron domains with PF5 and XeF4.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR predictions to molecules with expanded octets.
Identify trigonal bipyramidal and square planar molecular geometries.
instructions: Examine the axial and equatorial positions in these expanded octet molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Show PF5 to introduce 5 electron domains
clips.narration: Elements in period 3 and beyond can have expanded octets. Phosphorus pentafluoride (PF5) has five bonding domains, creating a trigonal bipyramidal geometry with axial and equatorial positions.

clips.changeMeaning: Show XeF4 to introduce 6 domains and lone pair placement
clips.narration: Finally, Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4) has six electron domains: four bonding and two lone pairs. To minimize repulsion, the lone pairs occupy opposite positions in the octahedral arrangement, resulting in a square planar molecular geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Wrap up lab and rotate both expanded octet molecules
clips.narration: By counting bonding and lone pairs, VSEPR theory accurately predicts the diverse 3D shapes of molecules, from simple tetrahedral structures to complex square planar geometries.
